extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors, poets, editors, and readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance on what makes worthwhile books, authorship, editorship, and poetry — including motives, labor, stylistic expectations, and how to cultivate young talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work must state a clear proposition or reveal a fact
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sir, what proposition is this book intended to set forth and commend? What fact does it reveal? What is its drift, its purport?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A book should embody a new truth or suggestion (even if mistaken) or else it is worthless. Works that merely resay what has been more forcibly or happily said already, and exist mainly to be "readable" and salable, should be denounced; only writings that disclose something substantive deserve encouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value new truths and original suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book "embodies a new truth, or even a new suggestion... make way for it! and let it fight its own battle".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty of proposition or suggestion merits allowance even when mistaken; the test is whether the work contributes new ideas or facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorship motivated by mere profit or publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a book's aim is merely "to be readable, therefore salable, and thus to win gold for its author... then let a bonfire be made of its manuscript sheets".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: writing primarily for fame, money, or marketability rather than truth or service. Such motive degrades literature and should be resisted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great writing requires intense devotion and patient labor
rubrics_metrics.description: "Eminence in any good or great undertaking implies intense devotion thereto, — implies patient, laborious exertion, either in the doing or in the preparing for it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Talent alone is insufficient; sustained study, painstaking revision, and refusal to publish until improved are markers of lasting quality (examples: Pope, Goldsmith, Gray studied and revised extensively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate and chasten youthful talent; withhold premature publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents should "read over his composition with him, and kindly point out its faults or weaknesses; encourage him to try again... but studiously withhold his productions from publicity".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage practice and correction rather than praise and early public exposure. Puffing a precocious child into public authorship risks ruining development; early failures are part of eventual improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor must serve the present but may choose conscience over popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Editor "must write to-day of to-day's incidents and aspects" and lives in the present; yet there is also a sterner path requiring advocacy for the wronged even at temporal cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two editorial modes: (a) the pragmatic editor who smooths and sidles to please public sentiment and survive; (b) the ideal editor who risks unpopularity to expose oppression and plunder — the latter sacrifices comfort for moral purpose and potential long-term moral reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty includes exposing social injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: A sterner editorial path "demands an ear ever open to the plaints of the wronged and the suffering... a pen as ready to expose and reprove the crimes whereby wealth is amassed and luxury enjoyed".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors choosing this path should expect annoyance from powerful interests and meagre temporal rewards but find recompense in conscience and the service to the despised and friendless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship must stem from service, not selfish or sordid motives
rubrics_metrics.description: "Literature is a noble calling, but only when the call obeyed by the aspirant issues from a world to be enlightened and blessed, not from a void stomach clamoring to be gratified and filled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should act from desire to serve and ennoble the race; selfish, sensual, or sordid motives are disqualifying and likely to corrupt the writer's faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain integrity and independence; avoid compromise for livelihood
rubrics_metrics.description: "Sell not your integrity; barter not your independence; beg of no man the privilege of earning a livelihood by Authorship... but, seeing through your own clear eyes, and uttering the impulses of your own honest heart, speak or write as truth and love shall dictate."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept material recompense that requires compromise of principle. If living by manual labor until genuine recompense arrives is necessary, prefer that to selling out. The test is whether accepting pay would imperil freedom or integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true poet's measure is moral and spiritual effect, not mere technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet's utterance "inspired the reader with a deeper and truer perception... impelled by it to love and practise virtue, to loathe vice, yet pity its victims..." then he was a true poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should move readers toward virtue, deeper perception, and human well-being. Technical originality without moral or spiritual effect is insufficient for true poetic greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is not equivalent to verse or rhyme
rubrics_metrics.description: "The most vulgar error... is that which somehow confounds [poetry] with verse, and even with rhyme... there is no more poetry in it than in the request, 'Pass me the baked potatoes.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme, measured metre, and conventional versification are fashions, not the essence. Great poets may not rhyme; rhyming facility is no proof of poetic genius (example: John Bunyan's doggerel versus his prose epic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelism is a natural and ancient poetic device
rubrics_metrics.description: "The oldest and most natural... form of poetic expression... is that of parallelism, or the expression of the same idea or sentiment through two succeeding images or affirmations" (example: Biblical passages and folk songs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallelism (cumulative/confirmatory repetition through images) is highlighted as a primitive, powerful poetic technique, especially in early literature and oral traditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern poets face strict critical canons; originality risks censure
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet of our day "must be an obedient vassal to an inexorable rule... must shun ruggedness or wilfulness... must respect the unities, and be loyal to rhythm and rhyme, — or he cannot induce the critics even to blast him with their thunders."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: defying critics' canons may yield temporary attention but risks being marginalized or 'tamed' by criticism. Examples: MacDonald Clarke and Walt Whitman faced critical resistance despite originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic temperament arises from certain life conditions (e.g., shepherd life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shepherds' loneliness, silence, and watchfulness predispose them to poetry; pastoral and rugged environments foster the poetic fire (example: Book of Job's pastoral origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/anthropological claim: environments that encourage reflection, solitude, and close observation are fertile for poetic development; such conditions inform imagery and perspective.
